claude.sample_unit: education topics (60 texts in four-group analysis)

links.outcome: Accuracy of LLM drafts versus clinician-reviewed LLM drafts (human-AI collaboration) rated against checklist
links.effect: Clinician-reviewed LLM drafts (Group D) accuracy 4.49 vs. unreviewed LLM texts (Group B) 3.23 (p<0.001); D matched clinician-only 4.48 (p=1.000); review took 5.1 min per text vs 18.5 min.
links.quote: Group C (4.48 ± 0.53) and Group D (4.49 ± 0.36) scored significantly higher than Group A (3.15 ± 0.78) and Group B (3.23 ± 0.69) (all p < 0.001).

links.outcome: Whether expert review corrects domain-specific errors in LLM-generated TCM and procedural content
links.effect: Expert-revised LLM texts improved accuracy from 3.23 to 4.49; TCM topics remained lowest across groups (Group C 3.8; Group D 4.0), and LLM TCM depth was limited.
links.quote: Critically, the human-AI collaboration model remediated these accuracy deficits, achieving accuracy equivalent to clinician-only texts.

links.outcome: Reading difficulty of original Chinese patient education materials versus LLM/clinician rewrites (sentence length)
links.effect: Original texts had longest sentences (33.9 characters) and university-level difficulty; LLM rewrite reduced to 21.1, clinician to 27.3, human-AI to 20.4 (all p<0.001).
links.quote: Group A had the longest sentences (33.9 ± 1.4 characters), followed by Group C (27.3 ± 2.0), Group B (21.1 ± 1.3), and Group D (20.4 ± 1.0).

links.outcome: Actionability (PEMAT) of plain-language LLM-rewritten materials versus original and clinician-written materials
links.effect: LLM actionability 95.6% vs original 16.7% and clinician 46.7%; human-AI 95.6%; no human-written text reached the 70% threshold.
links.quote: All four LLM subgroups scored significantly higher than both A and C (all p ≤ 0.002): GPT-4 (80.0% ± 22.2%, 7/15 ≥ 70%), Claude Opus 4.6 (95.6% ± 11.3%, 13/15 ≥ 70%), DeepSeek-V2 (97.8% ± 8.6%, 14/15 ≥ 70%), Gemini 3.0 pro (95.6% ± 11.3%, 13/15 ≥ 70%).

links.outcome: Consistency of LLM output actionability and accuracy across prompt styles (empathetic, concise, authoritative)
links.effect: Accuracy showed borderline gradient across prompts (2.53, 2.67, 2.80; p=0.050); all below clinician 4.00; actionability robust under empathetic/authoritative prompts but attenuated under concise prompt.
links.quote: Accuracy scores showed a borderline-significant gradient across the three prompt conditions (Friedman χ 2 (2) = 6.00, p = 0.050): Prompt A (2.53 ± 0.61), Prompt B (2.67 ± 0.46), Prompt C (2.80 ± 0.40).

links.outcome: Readability and actionability of patient materials
links.effect: LLM rewrites had shorter sentences, 21.1 vs 33.9 characters, and higher actionability, 95.6% vs 16.7%; both p < 0.001.
links.quote: LLM-rewritten texts demonstrated significantly shorter sentences (21.1 vs. 33.9 characters, p < 0.001) and substantially higher actionability (95.6% vs. 16.7%, p < 0.001) compared with original texts.

links.effect: Standalone Claude LLM accuracy was 3.23 ± 0.69, significantly lower than clinician 4.48 ± 0.53 and human-AI 4.49 ± 0.36; p < 0.001.
links.quote: Group C (4.48 ± 0.53) and Group D (4.49 ± 0.36) scored significantly higher than Group A (3.15 ± 0.78) and Group B (3.23 ± 0.69) (all p < 0.001).

links.effect: Accuracy varied across prompt styles: A 2.53 ± 0.61, B 2.67 ± 0.46, C 2.80 ± 0.40; Friedman χ2(2)=6.00, p=0.050.
links.quote: Accuracy scores showed a borderline-significant gradient across the three prompt conditions (Friedman χ 2 (2) = 6.00, p = 0.050): Prompt A (2.53 ± 0.61), Prompt B (2.67 ± 0.46), Prompt C (2.80 ± 0.40).
